item.content:encoded:
Lime-plastered brickwork, timber boards and cork panels were used to help capture the changing light at Pine House, a terraced home in London renovated by local architecture studio Polysmiths.

Located in Peckham, the project set out to tackle what Polysmiths founder Charles Wu described as the "well-known limitations" of London's ubiquitous Victorian terraces.

This included opening up the home's narrow plan by carving out an expansive double-height void at its centre.

"The problems of the Victorian terrace typology became the generative brief: long, narrow proportions, a compressed rear extension, and poor daylight penetration," Wu told Dezeen.

"The project is built around designing light itself as the primary material, to reinterpret the terrace into an open, generous home," he added.

"The guiding principle is that light needs shadow to exist. Textures and shadows are what give a space its atmosphere."

Key to creating a feeling of spaciousness in Pine House was establishing a single axis through its ground floor, connecting a reception room with a large bay window at the front to an angular glazed garden room sheltered by timber slats at the rear.

In between, the central kitchen and dining area sits at the base of the newly-created double-height void, illuminated by a row of windows to the south and overlooked by a small mezzanine library to the north.

"Rather than a conventional rear extension or side-return, we removed a mid-floor over the rear outrigger to create a double-height void, letting south-facing upper-level light fall through to the kitchen and living room," Wu told Dezeen.

"The rear elevation faces south-east, which we treated as an opportunity by angling the garden room glazing further south to soften that corner and pull in more light," he added.

Read:

Sunken lightwells illuminate partially submerged London home by Stylus Architects

The central space combines all the elements in Pine House's material palette, with lime-washed brick walls above, timber-lined walls and storage surrounding the kitchen, and cork boards used for the ceilings and garden room's walls.

On the first and second floors, across which four bedrooms and two bathrooms are organised, lime-washed brick walls are complemented by plastered surfaces, timber floors and tiled bathrooms.

"Interior walls were stripped to brick and given only a thin lime-plaster wash, creating a textured surface that catches changing shadow through the day," Wu explained.

"Solid Radiata Pine boards line the main living spaces for a warm, honey-toned glow; the garden room is lined in dark expanded cork boards, chosen so southern sunlight would create strong texture and shadow contrast," he added.

Facing the street, the home's facade has been kept the same, save for a slatted timber fence and storage area topped with planting.

​​Polysmiths was founded by Wu in 2017. Previous projects by the studio include the renovation of a home in Wanstead informed by Mediterranean villas and the redesign of a basement flat in Tufnell Park to feel like a "cabin in the woods".

The photography is by Lorenzo Zandri.

item.content:encoded:
Meta is creating a tiny, portable Muse Charm device for carrying around the company's AI agent, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has announced.

Produced by Meta's new design team, led by former Apple design chief Alan Dye, the device resembles an Apple Watch but with a small lanyard instead of a strap.

A customisable cartoon character occupies the entire two-inch screen, prompting comparisons to an AI-powered Tamagotchi.

This avatar acts as the cutesy embodiment of the Muse AI agent the company launched earlier this month, billed as a "personal assistant" that can automate daily admin such as writing emails and booking appointments, rather than just answering questions.

The Muse Charm features a fingerprint sensor in the corner that users can tap to start talking to the AI, with a built-in 5G modem for Wi-Fi-less internet access. There also appears to be a small camera, allowing the agent to take in information about the user's surroundings.

Read:

Sweekar is world's "first emotionally intelligent" pocket-sized pet

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg teased the product, set to go on sale ahead of the Christmas holidays, during the company's annual Meta Connect showcase, which also saw the launch of two new smart glasses.

"We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said in his keynote. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."

The avatar can be set to a menagerie of characters, from a Muse mascot known as "Jolly" to an anthropomorphic mango, a labradoodle and a piece of toast wearing sunglasses.

Combined with playing into Gen Z's love for bag charms and Labubu-style plushies, the device seems to be pitched at a younger demographic, who are already more likely to see AI bots as companions rather than mere helpers.

Meta's Muse AI has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch in early September, according to Sensor Tower data, and is set to be added to Meta smart glasses over the coming months.

The company does not have the best track record when it comes to handling private and sensitive information.

Read:

Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026

Meta Glasses have faced backlash for being used to film people – especially women – without their consent, and for sharing private videos captured by users with subcontractors in Kenya as part of training Muse AI.

These issues may be compounded by adding an AI agent into the mix and giving it eyes and ears. In the two weeks since its launch, Muse AI has already been accused of reading users' private messages, attempting to hack their Gmail and nudging them to share their passport information and bank account details.

Using cuteness as a way to encourage users to adopt a product they might otherwise be sceptical of is not new. Robotics companies have been following a similar playbook in recent years, with launches including fluffy robots that clip onto a handbag and emotionally intelligent AI pets.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio BDP has unveiled a pharmaceutical research campus in Shanghai, China, comprised of interconnected buildings that evoke the movement of cell division.

Located within Hongqiao International Central Business District in west Shanghai, the 186,000-square-metre research and development headquarters was developed for Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group (CTTQ), one of China's leading pharmaceutical companies.

BDP's design was informed by the structure of cells, with two pairs of interconnected buildings on the site.

Both pairs were designed to resemble cells splitting with glass covered bridges connecting them.

The cores of the two research buildings are split between either end of the buildings, allowing large and flexible floor plates for changing laboratory requirements.

One of the research buildings was connected to a smaller block containing staff accommodation, while the other one was connected to a taller administrative building.

The administrative building is the highest on the site, with the aim of creating a vocal point for the new headquarters. A conference centre is connected to this building.

"This is a place for research within a campus that doesn't turn its back on the city or the people using it," said BDP director Tianyi Gu.

"The central heart opens the site up to the public, while the buildings are planned to make research, collaboration and everyday life work together."

A raised sky bridge curves around the site to connect all the buildings on the campus as well as providing a series of indoor and outdoor spaces for people to meet and interact.

Cafes, a canteen and gym are located at the lower levels of the buildings, supporting the wellbeing of the staff and work-life balance.

Read:

KPF wraps China skyscraper in one-kilometer-long "landscape ribbon"

According to BDP, the arrangement of the four blocks was designed to break down the scale of the campus into a series of destinations.

"We've paid close attention to the things that make a difference to people's working day – access to daylight and fresh air, places to meet, eat and exercise, and spaces to step away from the laboratory," said Gu.

"For CTTQ, this is a research campus built for change, but also a place for people, a place with a strong sense of identity and an identifiable connection to Shanghai."

Passive design strategies were applied across the campus, including natural ventilation, facade solar shading, as well as customised facade designs responding to different orientations and functions.

Low-E glass was used to improve energy performance, while a large array of photovoltaic panels were installed on the roof, creating a unique pattern that add to the identity of the campus.

Elsewhere in China, KPF designed a tech campus in Shenzhen wrapped by a one-kilometer-long "landscape ribbon", while RSHP has completed a mixed-use skyscraper in Shanghai, informed by the city's historical laneway network.

The photography is courtesy of BDP.

Dezeen Showroom: recycled wool and renewable flax come together in a warm melange of colour in British textile brand Camira's ReSKU 2.0 fabric.

ReSKU 2.0 was launched to celebrate Camira's 50th anniversary in 2024 and inspired by the brand's original 1998 ReSKU fabric, made from recycled army jumpers.

For ReSKU 2.0, the brand combined recycled wool and polyamide generated from its own manufacturing waste with harvested flax, a renewable, low-carbon crop that grows with little water.

The process is conducted through Camira's textile recycling arm, iinouiio, which makes use of advanced textile reprocessing techniques, and the fabric it yields has a rich, tweedy look that showcases the natural colour variation of recycled materials.

ReSKU 2.0 is available in a choice of 24 shades. Camira says it is suitable for applications such as seating, curtains and panels, in settings including modern workplaces and hospitality venues.

"More than a fabric, ReSKU 2.0 represents a commitment to circular thinking and responsible manufacturing," said Camira.

"By turning production waste into a valuable resource, it demonstrates how heritage, innovation and sustainability can work together to create a textile that is recycled, renewable and ready for the future."

item.content:encoded:
Czech lighting brand Lasvit has preserved the forms of dried flowers inside hand-blown glass to create a large chandelier in a home in Napa Valley, California, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen for the brand.

Called Herbarium, the installation was made from dozens of individually crafted glass pieces suspended at different heights above the home's main living area.


Lasvit installed its Herbarium chandelier in a Napa Valley residence

Some of the glass pieces are long and slender, while others form rounded, teardrop-like shapes, creating a loose cascade that extends towards the floor.

Each piece was made by placing dried flowers and plants beneath molten glass. The heat consumes the organic material while leaving its impression embedded in the crystal.

"Our glassworks are surrounded by wild nature," said Lasvit chief designer Mária Čulenová, who led the creative team behind the installation.

"With Herbarium, we wanted to capture this wilderness so that anyone could take home a piece of this landscape – a piece of the meadow, preserved in glass."

The chandelier occupies the centre of the double-height living room, where it hangs in front of a large window overlooking the surrounding landscape.

Its clear and amber-toned pieces catch both daylight and artificial illumination, casting irregular shadows across the pale walls.

The residence sits in Napa Valley, surrounded by vineyards, wildflowers and a stream running through the property.

Inside, the Herbarium installation echoes the vegetation visible through the windows, preserving its forms in glass.

Herbarium is part of Lasvit Icons, a collection of the Czech glassmaker's designs adapted into modular systems.

Rather than producing every installation entirely from scratch, the system uses individually handcrafted components that can be configured for different interiors, from private homes to larger architectural projects.

Founded in 2007 by Leon Jakimič, Lasvit specialises in bespoke lighting, glass installations and architectural glass, combining traditional Bohemian glassmaking with contemporary design.

Other projects by Lasvit featured on Dezeen include its 2025 Soaked in Light exhibition, which featured a splash-shaped installation and glass light imprinted with a tree branch.

item.content:encoded:
Sewn paper and hand-hammered steel sit side by side in these lighting pieces and stools by designer Jesse Butterfield, displayed during London Design Festival 2026.

The aptly named Sew Paper Lighting and Stool Des Pois series premiered during Butterfield's A Veil Boundary exhibition, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker, in the city-wide festival's Brompton Design District.

The paper lanterns continue the centuries-old tradition of using the material to make lampshades, as a result of its physical lightness as well as its translucency.

To realise the Sew Paper Lighting series, Butterfield teamed up with The Paper Foundation, a Lake District-based paper mill, founded by sixth-generation papermaker Mark Cropper.

"We got to visit The Paper Foundation and see their process, then select six or seven different papers," said Butterfield.

"We went through their archive and chose what we thought would have nice drapage and lighting effects, as well as selecting different papers for different applications."

Slim stainless steel frames dictate each piece's general form and purpose: from pendants and wall lights to floor and table lamps.

Beyond this, the lanterns strewn around the space comprise folded, draped and otherwise physically manipulated handmade paper, hand-stitched into amorphous shapes.

Read:

RCA design students exercise restraint in One Tool One Stool exhibition

In dialogue with the paper lamps, Butterfield's Stool Des Pois series explores the sheet metal's capacity to behave in a similar way to paper.

A paper model was the natural starting point for the stool, which was then scaled up and recreated in steel, heated and hammered by hand until a thinness and lightness akin to paper was achieved.

The stools are based on the same initial model and dimensions, with natural variations owing to their handmade nature, ensuring that no two are entirely alike.

Further distinction is made through the polka dot patterning, a result of intentional blackening of the metal which introduces further visual interest while telling the story of their manufacturing process.

"This is the first time where I'm leaving the dots on the surface," said Butterfield.

"They come from the making process – in the past I've sanded them away, but I wanted to bring them in now as they fit with the theme of things being perfectly imperfect," he added, nodding to the leitmotif of this year's Brompton Design District programme.

Elsewhere in the district, RCA students exhibited a series of stools created with a single tool and Isamaya French launched her second-ever Studio Iron show.

The photography is by Andy Stagg.

A Veil Boundary was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a sleep support device that encourages users to record valuable moments of their day is among the projects from students at Georgia Institute of Technology.

Also featured is a compact bike that can store groceries, and a smartphone game to help improve understanding of sustainability.

Georgia Institute of Technology

Institution: School of Industrial Design
Courses: Master in Industrial Design Project and Product Development and Innovation
Tutors: Leila Aflatoony, EunSook Kwon, Herb Velazquez, Wayne Li, HyunJoo Oh and Kevin Shankwiler

School statement:

"The School of Industrial Design at Georgia Tech prepares students to address complex societal and innovation challenges through the integration of design, research and technology.

"As one of the world's leading research universities, we view industrial design as a discipline that generates knowledge and creates solutions.

"Our students and faculty explore the relationships among people, technology, society and business, using research to inform innovation and improve lives.

"Through collaboration across disciplines, students learn to navigate complexity and create solutions that are technically feasible and socially meaningful.

"Our programmes combine the creative foundations of design with research, technological fluency and interdisciplinary collaboration. Students learn to understand human needs, translate insights into action and develop meaningful solutions.

"The School of Industrial Design offers bachelor's and master's degrees, and our new PhD in integrated design and computing. Our programmes are recognised as human-centred technology design STEM degrees.

"The inherently interdisciplinary nature of design thinking and design research, combined with students' diverse academic and professional backgrounds, creates an educationally rich environment of interdisciplinary collaboration.

"Our curriculum fortifies the designer's role in humanising connections between people and technology, with a focus on the areas of interaction design, healthcare design, service design, product design and user-experience research."

Fresh! Bicycle by Aiden Soriano, Futa Kakinuma, Han Zheng, Leif Horn and Vu Ly

"The Fresh! Bicycle is a novel electric bicycle that transforms into a shopping platform.

"By enabling the bike to fold to nearly half its size, we address the issue of excessive lateral space when parked. This compact form makes Fresh! easier to store, park and navigate within tight urban environments.

"Fresh! streamlines shopping into a simple in-and-out experience. Instead of leaving products exposed, the bike keeps groceries safe, visible and directly in front of the rider.

"Fresh! affords freedom to move between stores or to a picnic without constantly loading and unloading items, expanding use beyond a single grocery trip."

Students: Aiden Soriano, Futa Kakinuma, Han Zheng, Leif Horn and Vu Ly
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler

Ducati Pen by Vu Ly

"'In lightness, my strength,' is Ducati's motto, embodying its relentless pursuit of style, sophistication and performance.

"The Ducati Trio Draft translates superbike architecture into an advanced three-in-one multi-pen and pencil."

Student: Vu Ly
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio I
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler

Mobster Wet/Dry Vac for Ridgid by Yhali Sheba

"The Mobster Wet/Dry Vacuum for Ridgid presents a unique and innovative 'upside-down' concept for job site cleaning.

"By moving the motor to the bottom of the unit, the drum can be modularised to fit varying capacities.

"Additionally, the Mobster has a trash hatch on the lid, allowing workers to toss in debris that may be too big for a vacuum hose to handle."

Student: Yhali Sheba
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio I
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler

Cadence Bicycle by Aisling Mahony, Estelle Cole, Serena McGuinn and Yhali Sheba

"Cadence is an electrically-assisted shared-use bicycle that incorporates music to build community.

"With an adaptive digital audio system, it allows you to mix music with friends and other bikers as you ride. Cadence transforms the experience of bike rental, taking it from transportation to a journey riders look forward to.

"Additionally, Cadence enables ride adaptability with the inclusion of a rear seat and fold-down footrest, allowing riders to use the bike beyond their ride during standstill moments and retaining it throughout the whole trip."

Students: Aisling Mahony, Estelle Cole, Serena McGuinn and Yhali Sheba
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler

Pik Bicycle by Arya Deshmukh, Cierra Langer, Kesiah Munyaruganda and Mia Wood

"The Pik Bicycle began as an exploration of shared mobility and became an argument for belonging. By treating the bike as a canvas rather than a commodity, we designed a system that adapts to people, stories and cities in motion.

"This project shows that shared transportation doesn't have to feel anonymous.

"Pik is built around choice and adaptability, reflecting how riders pick their mode  – solo, shared or cargo – while the lighting system enables personal expression.

"Combined with ride documentation, the brand turns each trip into a personal and memorable experience. Your Pik is a piece of you."

Students: Arya Deshmukh, Cierra Langer, Kesiah Munyaruganda and Mia Wood
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler

Scrapling by Feiyang Liu

"Scrapling is a hybrid mobile game designed to help people understand sustainability through everyday interaction.

"The core concept centres on by-product circulation – the idea that materials often considered waste in production systems still hold value and potential.

"In the game, industrial by-products are personified as collectable characters called Scraplings. Each Scrapling represents a real-world by-product (e.g., wood residue, fly ash, whey) and interacts with the player through short dialogue-based quiz questions."

Student: Feiyang Liu
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: EunSook Kwon
Email: fliu358[at]gatech.edu

Oris by Vedant Kulkarni

"Oris reframes outdoor safety as a continuous, ambient layer of protection rather than a reactive tool of last resort. The device monitors movement, heart rate and location, initiating an alert sequence if prolonged inactivity is detected during a trek.

"This escalating model, progressing from haptic check-in to emergency beacon, transforms Oris from passive monitor to active guardian."

Student: Vedant Kulkarni
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: Herb Velazquez
Email: vkulkarni71[at]gatech.edu

Co Auronix by Yuanxiang Guo

"Co Auronix is an aftermarket control accessory for touchscreen vehicle human-machine interfaces that enables more convenient long-form audio listening and control while driving.

"Co Auronix demonstrates how a dedicated tangible interface can reduce visual demand, support safer driver behaviour and enhance the overall in-car listening experience.

"This design contributes to the broader discussion of automotive human-machine interaction by presenting an alternative to touchscreen-dominant systems, emphasising the value of tactile interaction for emerging in-car media experiences."

Student: Yuanxiang Guo
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: Wayne Li
Email: yuanxiangguo97[at]gmail.com

OrthoCore by Ruijie Jin

"Access to effective rehabilitation is limited by high costs, workforce shortages and insufficient therapy intensity, while existing robotic systems remain inaccessible due to their expense and complexity.

"OrthoCore presents an open-source modular rehabilitation robotics platform that integrates robotic joint modules, a guided parametric interface and customisable 3D-printed components to support personalised therapy."

Student: Ruijie Jin
Course: Master in Industrial Design Thesis
Tutor: Leila Aflatoony
Email: rjin71[at]gatech.edu

Somna by Yunhao Hua

"Somna proposes a reimagined sleep-support device as a day-night emotional anchor system that bridges daytime awareness and nighttime support.

"Rather than functioning as a passive sound masker, the system encourages users to intentionally record meaningful environmental moments during daily routines.

"These self-curated sounds are later replayed during periods of nighttime rumination, fostering a sense of familiarity, emotional grounding and continuity in lived experience.

"By transforming everyday auditory moments into personalised emotional anchors, the design supports subtle, non-clinical emotional regulation and redefines the role of sleep-aid sound devices from functional tools to experience-driven companions."

Student: Yunhao Hua
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: HyunJoo Oh
Email: yhua67[at]gatech.edu

Mexican practice Estudio Zero has created a co-living apartment building rendered in pink-toned concrete with a series of arched forms informed by sound waves in Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca.

Known as Amplitude Coliving, the 390-square-metre complex was completed in 2025 on a 315.5-square-metre site in La Punta, a coastal neighbourhood known for small-scale, independent construction.

Estudio Zero, which is based in Querétaro, worked with the client to personify the idea of amplitude, the physical shape of sound waves and the way energy travels and grows in intensity.

"We took that literally and translated it into the architecture – you can actually read the waveform in the facade, in the way the arches and columns rise and taper," the studio told Dezeen, explaining that the design also represents the energy of the client.

"From there it became a shared language between client and studio – not just a form, but a way of thinking about how energy and community move through the building."

The complex is organised as a sequence of courtyards, open-air corridors and interconnected common areas that allow circulation to progress into levels of social interaction.

A courtyard sits at the centre of the plan with a pool, shared kitchen and dining area and serves as the social heart of the complex. In the co-living plan, individuals rent rooms and share the common spaces.

"That's the whole idea behind this coliving model," the studio said, "not to program those encounters, but to design a courtyard that gives people every reason to be in the same place and let the connection happen on its own."

Open-air balconies with scalloped railings line the courtyard and transition to three different apartment types – studios, larger units with private garden spaces and double-height loft units on the upper level of the main facade with alternative roof vaults.

Tied to the Oaxacan coastal landscape, the interior and exterior colour palette includes terracotta-pink, hand-rendered stucco, board-formed concrete and tropical hardwood doors, window frames and custom millwork.

Read:

Productora models Oaxacan hotel suites after pre-Hispanic pyramids

The warm, natural materials contrast with glass block that filters light in the bedroom, delicate steel spiral staircases and cable railings that add a nautical touch to the mass.

"The tapered, hourglass-shaped concrete columns that flare out to meet the balcony slab. Visually, they read almost like a waveform, tying the structural language directly back to the 'amplitude' concept," the studio said, explaining that all of the details reinforce the idea of the building as something in motion rather than a static object.

Opposing openings, shaded open-air corridors, deep overhangs and spatial porosity keep air flowing through the building, while the thermal mass of the concrete and stucco moderates internal temperature swings.

Meanwhile, solar panels are paired with battery storage to keep the building running during tropical weather events.

Other recent projects in Mexico that deploy a similar pink scheme include a residential complex by V Taller in Tulum centred around a tower, blocky beach housing by Reyes Rios + Larrain in Dzemul and a renovated apartment building by Heryco in Queretaro.

The photography is by Alex Krotkov.

item.content:encoded:
Brooklyn creative studio MSCHF has created two twisted and bent versions of Lexus electric cars for New York City's fall art week, which the studio said is a play on the automotive industry's concept car prototypes.

The Motomorphosis sculptures, called Circle Car and Twisted Car, were installed at Hudson Yards event space Chelsea Industrial next to their functional counterparts, a Lexus RZ450e and Lexus RX450h+.

Circle Car is an elongated Lexus RZ450e turned around on itself, while Twisted Car looks like a Lexus RX450h+ that has been twisted and wrung out like a giant mechanical towel.

The team said Motomorphosis plays on the idea of a concept car, a prototype vehicle presented by car companies to showcase innovations in technology and style as an indicator of the company's direction.

"We had this idea of inverting the idea of a concept car and taking a purely formalist approach to the object," MSCHF chief creative officer Kevin Wiesner told Dezeen.

The forms were based around the impossible 3D formulations in digital design software.

"In this case, operations like twisting, stretching, and bending are part of a standard 3D program language that results in impossible objects; native digitally, but absurd physically," said Wiesner.

Read:

MSCHF creates furniture collection from "pile of car parts"

"Circle Car also taps into a specifically implied absurdity of movement; no matter how much it drives, it remains in one place chasing its own tail," he continued.

"Twist Car is one of those shapes that is taken directly from 3D software operations, though this degree of twist usually shows up as a visually compelling mistake."

The sculptures are made from a steel armature, with "thousands of individual pieces joined together like LEGOs to form the skin". While they incorporate some Lexus car parts, they are non-functioning and do not turn on, according to the studio.

Previously, MSCHF created furniture from Mercedes-AMG vehicle parts and cut a Gufram Pratone chair into little bits.

The photography is courtesy of MSCHF.

Motomorphosis is on display at Chelsea Industrial from 25 to 26 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events, exhibitions and installations around the world.

Dezeen School Shows: a centre for developing handmade paper is among the projects from students at Swinburne University of Technology.

Also featured is a tool to support those living with dementia and a mural that reflects the role of women and technology in the design industry.

Swinburne University of Technology

Institution: School of Design and Architecture
Courses: Bachelor of Design, Bachelor of Design (Communication Design, Hons), Bachelor of Design (Architecture), Bachelor of Design (Fashion), Bachelor of Design (Industrial Design, Hons), Bachelor of Design (Interior Architecture, Hons), Master of Architecture, Master of Architecture and Urban Design, Master of Design, Bachelor of Engineering (Architectural, Hons) and Bachelor of Engineering (Product Design, Hons)
Tutors: Simon Bronson, Jane Connory, Nicholas Chia, Phuong Quoc Dinh, Julia English, Sebastianus Funke Genaamd Kupper, Joanna Gardener, Peter Hvala, Markus Jung, Debra Kunda, Antony Linden, Simon Lloyd, Morganna Magee, Andrew Milward-Bason, Diego Munoz, Michele Murray, Charlie Ranscombe, Mark Strachan, Fanny Suhendra and Shivani Tyagi

School statement:

"At Swinburne's School of Design and Architecture, we empower creative thinkers to shape a better future. Our world-class education and research connect design, technology and industry to address real-world challenges and create meaningful impact.

"We explore emerging technologies, design for health and wellbeing, and sustainable approaches to the way we live, work and interact.

"Our courses are grounded in design history, culture, diversity and critical thinking, encouraging students and researchers to collaborate across disciplines and engage with global issues.

"Our graduates are recognised around the world for their creativity, innovation and leadership, making Swinburne ready to make a difference."

Park Weave by Brendan David O'Mahony and Pablo de Lascurain Zambrano

"Research into 106 John Street identified Brunswick East's transition from a low-density residential and industrial suburb to a series of transit-oriented urban centres focused on public transport, walking and cycling.

"This change is driven by an increasing population of highly educated adults aged 25 to 39, who now comprise 44.9 per cent of residents.

"In response to higher rates of de facto relationships, fewer children and elderly residents, the proposal delivers medium-density housing with adaptable shared spaces that support evolving household structures, including multigenerational living.

"By balancing private living with meaningful shared spaces, the project creates enduring social value and supports a more connected, adaptable and sustainable Brunswick East."

Students: Brendan David O'Mahony and Pablo de Lascurain Zambrano
Course: Bachelor of Design (Architecture)
Tutor: Debra Kunda
Email: brendan.o.drafting[at]gmail.com and plascurainz[at]gmail.com

Mutt. A Comic-Inspired Typeface. by Kina Kavak

"This project explored the role of typography in sustaining and reactivating print culture within Melbourne's contemporary design landscape.

"It investigated how typography could re-engage Melbourne's creative community with printed media in an increasingly digital environment.

"The project developed a typographic system and advertising identity for Studio Archive, culminating in a physical exhibition of typefaces and printed materials.

"The exhibition emphasised the tactile and spatial qualities of print, encouraging audiences to engage with design beyond the screen.

"Together, these outcomes formed a cohesive communication design campaign that positioned typography as a cultural medium celebrating Melbourne's independent print and street art communities."

Student: Kina Kavak
Course: Bachelor of Design – Communication Design
Tutor: Michele Murray
Email: kk[at]nakina.world

Group project: Modular Laser-Cut Garments

"Laser cutting offers new approaches to both manufacturing and design for fashion, as instead of relying on mass manufacturing, you can now create hyper-local and made-on-demand production.

"You can start to ask how laser cutting can create new experiences, from downloadable modular patterns and open-source design to etching and customisation for unique customer engagement strategies.

"We can design not only products, but innovative approaches to design and manufacturing for a technologically driven future for the Australian fashion industry."

Group: Emerging Technologies in Fashion and Textile Design Class of 2026
Course: Bachelor of Design (Fashion)
Tutor: Julia English
Email: jjenglish[at]swin.edu.au

Mira Living by Giulia Cilotti Bueno

"Mira Living is a line of products designed to support people living with dementia and their caregivers to co-manage and maintain routine.

"The ecosystem includes Mira Home, an e-ink display that emits gentle task reminders around the house; Mira Go, a portable version that guides users through activities outside the home; and Mira Board, a magnetic board that enables patients and caregivers to build their routine in a fully analogue way.

"By combining digital and tactile tools, Mira Living promotes cognitive engagement, helps build independence and eases caregiver burden, creating a more engaging and dignified environment for life with dementia."

Student: Giulia Cilotti Bueno
Course: Bachelor of Design (Industrial Design) (Hons)
Tutors: Charlie Ranscombe and Nicholas Chia
Email: giuliacbueno[at]uol.com.br

Made/Human by Alyssa Payad

"Made/Human explores the role of analogue making in a design landscape increasingly shaped by automation, precision and artificial intelligence (AI).

"Developed through a publication and interactive exhibition, the project reframes analogue processes as tools for emotional expression, material exploration and meaningful connection.

"Combining design-led research, material experimentation and contributions from practising designers, each publication explores relationships between specific analogue methods, materials and emotional tones, revealing diverse visual languages and interpretative possibilities.

"Made/Human advocates for hybrid creative practices that balance digital efficiency with embodied knowledge, human values and the expressive possibilities of making by hand."

Student: Alyssa Payad
Course: Bachelor of Design (Communication Design) (Hons)
Tutors: Shivani Tyagi and Fanny Suhendra
Email: alpadesignmelb[at]gmail.com

Beyond the Senses: An Exhibition Journey Through Healing Spaces by Joice Gia Linh Nguyen

"This project reimagines spatial experience as a means of supporting emotional recovery and well-being in modern life.

"Drawing upon the five human senses – sight, sound, touch, scent and taste – it translates therapeutic principles into immersive environments that evoke calm, awareness and self-reflection.

"Located in Port Melbourne, the exhibition unfolds along a guided pathway through five stages of psychological recovery. Each spatial cluster explores a distinct sensory experience, gradually shifting emotions from tension toward tranquillity.

"Extending beyond these senses, a sixth sense, an interior garden, creates a contemplative landscape that encourages connection, pause, reflection and inner clarity.

"Ultimately, the project envisions interior architecture as a non-verbal form of therapy, where sensory perception becomes a gentle guide toward healing and balance."

Student: Joice Gia Linh Nguyen
Course: Bachelor of Design (Interior Architecture) (Hons)
Tutors: Phuong Quoc Dinh and Simon Lloyd
Email: ndglinh1507[at]gmail.com

BrickHaus by Nam Bui

"BrickHaus by Nam Bui applies the Baugruppe development model to a three-storey apartment building in Brunswick, Melbourne. Replacing two detached houses, the proposal accommodates 15 dwellings alongside a shared rental space and flexible workshop.

"Curved brick facades bring warmth and texture while carefully arranged external circulation enables cross-ventilation, privacy and generous outlooks.

"Two co-apartments use shared kitchens and operable walls to balance community and privacy while reducing floor area and construction costs.

"Minimal car parking preserves space for landscaping and tree planting, while car-share spaces and secure bicycle parking support more sustainable patterns of urban living within a compact site."

Student: Nam Bui
Course: Master of Architecture
Tutor: Andrew Milward-Bason

Growth Lines by Sara Manfre and Ellie McGhee

"Growth Lines explores how architecture and landscape can support climate adaptation in Hawke's Bay (New Zealand) while protecting the productive landscapes central to the region's economy.

"Facing increasing risks from flooding, sea-level rise, extreme rainfall and changing growing conditions, the proposal reimagines relocation as an opportunity for renewal rather than retreat.

"The low-lying coastal community of Clive gradually moves inland along the river through a connected network of housing, public spaces and productive landscapes.

"Water acts as critical infrastructure, capturing seasonal flows to sustain agriculture year-round. Developed across three adaptive phases, the project demonstrates how resilient communities can grow, thrive and prosper in response to climate change."

Students: Sara Manfre and Ellie McGhee
Course: Master of Architecture and Urban Design
Tutor: Markus Jung
Email: 103956041[at]student.swin.edu.au and 103861284[at]student.swin.edu.au

Group project: Monster Mural – Women, Technology and Teratology in Design

"As part of the Master of Design at Swinburne University, students were challenged to design an individual 40 by 40 centimetre mural tile exploring women, technology and teratology in design.

"Each tile investigated overlooked women in design, emerging technologies and the idea of the 'monster' as a metaphor for challenging social and technological boundaries.

"Using digital fabrication technologies in the ProtoLAB, students created layered spatial artworks that combined into a permanent collaborative mural, transforming a university space into a public statement advocating for gender equity, critical design thinking and creative experimentation."

Students: Bhanush Bhaskar Shetty, Steven Connelly, Cori Emmolo, Gayani Kaushalya Wijesekara, Ganitharathna Banjanayalage, Sofie Svele Graee, Mishka Greene, Zitong (Tommy) He, Nakyoung (Loha) Heo, Kimhour Hok, Chintong Hor, Denis Kiprop, Amith Paul, Soksan Seak, Stephy Ann Shibu, Maxwell Tong, Thi Ngan Giang (Janet) Tran, Jiannan Wang and Buddhika Ranmini (Minnie) Wijesinghage
Course: Master of Design
Tutors: Jane Connory, Niqui Toldi, Maia Kjendle, Elliot Henkel and Ravi Bessabava

Loop de Loop by Jerry Nguyen

"Jerry Nguyen's Loop de Loop showcases the creativity, technical craft and visual experimentation developed through Swinburne's Motion Design programme.

"Created in response to a brief exploring energy through an infinite 3D loop, the work transforms music into a continuously evolving visual experience.

"A spinning record player opens into kaleidoscopic tunnels, musicians, abstract forms and bursts of light before seamlessly returning to its beginning.

"Through bold colour, stylised 3D modelling, lighting, animation and carefully choreographed transitions, Jerry demonstrates how motion design can combine storytelling, sound and digital image-making to create distinctive, immersive visual worlds."

Student: Jerry Nguyen
Course: Bachelor of Design/Communication Design – Motion Design
Tutor: Simon Bronson
Email: quangcanh.jb367[at]gmail.com

SyriSter UV-C Sterilisation for Syringes by Hannah Gough

"Worldwide, 40 per cent of all injections are delivered using unsterile, re-used syringes, causing 1.3 million preventable deaths per year.

"The SyriSter is a sterilisation device for syringes, targeted for use in disaster/crisis zones and hospitals that are economically disadvantaged or in crisis.

"In these circumstances, syringe re-use is common or necessary practice. The SyriSter aims to make this practice safer through reliable UV-C sterilisation to remove the risk of pathogen and disease transmission between patients.

"The design focuses on usability, field-use practicality and design for manufacture. SyriSter has been recognised with the James Dyson Award and was a winner in the Australian Good Design Awards' Next Gen category."

Student: Hannah Gough
Course: Bachelor of Engineering (Product Design) (Hons)
Tutors: Mark Strachan, Sebastianus Funke Genaamd Kupper and Peter Hvala
Email: hannah_gough[at]outlook.com

The Immigration Museum Re-Imagined by Alex Cox

"Developed as part of an industry brief to re-imagine Melbourne's Immigration Museum through a fresh visual lens, these two images from a larger series trace the layered, moving experience of the city of Melbourne.

"This treatment positions colour itself as a kind of migration: moving through, layering over and connecting disparate parts of the city, echoing journeys of arrival and passage rather than illustrating them literally.

"Alex's treatment of the brief allowed for a new dynamic reading of the importance of the journey and the destination."

Student: Alex Cox
Course: Bachelor of Design/Communication Design – Photography
Tutor: Morganna Magee
Email: alexcoxfhd[at]gmail.com

Intake Nutrition Tracking Dashboard by Joleen Adriana Gandakusuma

"Intake is a nutrition tracking dashboard designed to make daily food and nutrition logging clearer, more accessible and easier to maintain.

"The project was developed through an iterative research and design process, beginning with literature and competitor analysis, followed by handmade prototyping and focus group testing.

"Insights from testing informed the structure, interactions and visual design of the final dashboard. The experience prioritises reducing cognitive load while presenting nutritional information in a way that is simple to understand and act upon.

"Through a combination of research, interaction design and visual communication, Intake explores how thoughtful dashboard design can make everyday health tracking feel more intuitive and manageable."

Student: Joleen Adriana Gandakusuma
Course: Bachelor of Design/Communication Design – UX Interaction Design
Tutors: Antony Linden and Diego Munoz
Email: joleenadriana[at]gmail.com

Paper Nest by DucThang Pham

"Paper Nest reimagines handmade papermaking as a contemporary spatial experience.

"Inspired by the woven structure of a bird's nest, the project brings together craft, community and sustainability through organic forms, natural textures and a handcrafted visual identity.

"Conceived as a 'home of handmade paper', visitors experience the transformation of discarded fibres into paper, objects and artworks through making, touch and observation."

Student: DucThang Pham
Course: Bachelor of Design/Communication Design – Experiential Design
Tutors: Joanna Gardener and Simon Lloyd
Email: ducthang.des[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
Swiss studio Herzog & de Meuron has utilised the existing concrete foundation of an older structure for the Student Center & Dining Commons at Amherst College, adding mass-timber levels on top.

The Student Center & Dining Commons at Amherst College in Massachusetts rises from the skeleton of the Merrill Science Center, a brutalist brick building designed in the 1960s by Boston firm Campbell, Aldrich and Nulty.

Herzog & de Meuron expanded the building from 80,000 to 120,000 square feet (7,432 to 11,148 square metres) to accommodate a combined student centre and dining hall. It also opened up the site to give views that were previously blocked by the brutalist building. The studio worked with Sasaki, which served as executive architect.

The McGuire building, which abutted the Merrill Science Center, was demolished.

"Although it was originally adjacent to the quad, its position became increasingly obstructive over time," said the studio.

"From the outset, the aim was to avoid repeating this condition and create a more open, modest building in dialogue with the campus."

The foundation of the existing building already navigated the slope from the quad to the greenspace, so, in order to meet the carbon neutrality goals of Amherst, the studio opted to use the existing concrete foundations.

Two lower-level foundations were kept with two levels added on top.

The upper levels were clad in a lightly oiled Western Red Cedar, while the lower levels were clad in cedar that was stained almost completely black. This "eggplant" tone was designed to create a sense of gradation from dark to light with the slope, highlighting the upper-level additions.

Throughout, deep eaves were built onto the structure, creating solar shading and shelter on the outdoor areas on the third and fourth levels.

Mass-timber structural columns were attached to the pre-existing concrete ones with timber spaces using a split-beam and corbel connection.

This connection occurs on the second level, making it a hybrid timber-concrete structure, while the third and fourth levels are almost completely made of mass timber, which was derived from Canadian Black Spruce.

A large rooftop social area was created on top of the third level, where a series of low-lying pavilion structures were placed. These buildings hold a black-box theatre and a variety of religious buildings.

An atrium on the top level lets light into the circular opening. The third level holds study spaces and event spaces and also has a winter garden courtyard hemmed in by glass so that light can filter in from above.

On the third level, the studio placed the primary entrance level with the upper quad. From here, a central hallway navigates the slope of the site down to the first-level entrance at the green space.

This passageway runs through a circular opening that was created in the concrete floor plate of the third level.

Most of the dining functions were placed on the first two levels. The social hallway leads down into larger lobby spaces on the first and second floors.

Another interesting cutaway was placed on the transition from the first to the second, with panes of glass added above the primary passageway to open up views into the dining area.

Wood details such as a gridded ceiling treatment and walls were included on the second level. At other points, mostly on the first level, concrete was left exposed.

This first level features additional dining spaces, a mailroom, as well as a pub, which was clad in the same dark timber as the lower exterior.

As the building reconnects the campus, the studio said it also conceptually links it to the school's carbon-neutral future goals.

"The project links the site's history to Amherst College's future — creating communal spaces for student life and wellbeing and pursuing climate action as a shared priority," said Herzog & de Meuron partner-in-charge Christoph Röttinger.

Read:

Herzog & de Meuron designs own offices in Basel as a "repository of materials"

The architecture studio claimed a 33 per cent reduction in embodied carbon compared to a similar building size and type, as well as a 93 per cent reduction in operational carbon. This efficient operation was partly enabled by the arrays of solar panels placed on the pavilion structures on the fourth level.

It was also Herzog & de Meuron's first educational building completed in the United States.

The studio recently completed the Calder Gardens art museum in Philadelphia.

The studio was also tapped, alongside EHDD, to convert the former Birkenstock campus in California into a design museum for the Eames Institute.

The photography is by Iwan Baan.

item.content:encoded:
Swiss architect Peter Zumthor has expanded the Fondation Beyeler museum in Riehen, Switzerland, with a cluster of art buildings designed to nestle into the park setting.

Built in the gardens outside the original Fondation Beyeler art museum, which was designed by Renzo Piano in 1997, the trio of buildings include a rammed-concrete art gallery, a glazed cultural space and a wood-clad office building.

Rather than combine all the functions into one building, Zumthor's studio Atelier Peter Zumthor chose to scatter them across the museum's park to help them blend into the surroundings.

"I wanted my buildings to blend in so naturally that it felt completely self-evident," said Zumthor.

"It makes me happy when people now tell me they look as if they've always been here," he continued.

"From the outside, the buildings sit beautifully on the site, and inside, they have large, airy spaces that don't feel formulaic – they are wonderfully expressive, beautiful spaces."

The three-storey Wyss Museum has a Y-shaped floor plan that avoids existing trees and contains exhibition space with large, bronze-framed windows overlooking the surrounding foliage.

Its walls are made from rammed concrete with Jura limestone aggregate, which gives the facades a warm yellow tone.

Jura limestone also appears in the building's terrazzo flooring, benches, and solid stone staircase wrapping the building core, which contains the cloakroom and elevator.

The top floor of the Wyss Museum opens onto a roof terrace, where visitors are guided to the rear gardens via a staircase that offers glimpses of the greenery through triangular wall openings.

Read:

Photos reveal Peter Zumthor's LACMA museum ahead of opening

The Ammann Pavilion is a one-storey building designed as a public lounge and space to host cultural events, such as performances, talks and film screenings.

Glass walls in oak frames immerse the building in the surrounding park.

Cherry and pear wood surfaces add warmth to the interior, which features stepped flooring that doubles as auditorium seats.

Art logistics facilities and offices are located in the Erlen Torhaus building, which is connected to the existing museum by an underground corridor.

Artwork deliveries are processed on the ground floor, which is clad in varnished oak, while workspaces on the upper floors have large windows overlooking the surroundings.

As part of the Fondation Beyeler expansion, Atelier Peter Zumthor worked with Vogt Landscape Architects on the landscaping of the park, which was populated with outdoor artworks by artists Louise Bourgeois, Pierre Huyghe and Rachel Whiteread.

Alongside Zumthor's trio of buildings, early 19th-century buildings elsewhere in the museum complex have been restored and updated for new uses.

French architect India Mahdavi transformed the Orangerie building to accommodate a greenhouse and adjoining shop for plant enthusiasts, exposing the original timber roof structure and adding light-green accents.

Swiss studio Forsberg Architekten updated the museum's Ammann Atelier to provide workspaces for art education and workshops, and created a music listening lounge with a tessellating acoustic ceiling in the adjacent Salon room.

The expanded Fondation Beyeler will have a preliminary opening with limited visitation from 26 September, before fully opening to the public on 15 January 2027.

Earlier this year, Zumthor's long-awaited Los Angeles County Museum of Art expansion opened to the public, with artworks displayed in its large, snaking concrete structure.

His other notable projects include Secular Retreat – a holiday home in Devon formed from rammed concrete.

item.content:encoded:
Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio.

Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its market-leading range of eyewear and headsets.

The Meta VR Glasses represent the bigger breakthrough, bringing virtual-reality gaming, 3D movies and other immersive digital experiences into a form factor only slightly larger than an ordinary pair of glasses.

This allows them to be worn for longer than current headsets and carried on the daily commute, as people might do with a pair of over-ear headphones.

Meta says it achieved the lightweight construction by splitting the architecture into two: the glasses, weighing about 100 grams, plus an attached "puck" that clips onto a pocket or bag and handles the processing.

Also key are the glasses' ultra-compact pancake lenses, which are about the size of a Scrabble tile and are fixed within a soft mesh structure on the inside of the frames.

The wearer manually shifts these lenses to sit directly in front of their eye, filling everything but their peripheral view with a 5K display.

This micro-OLED display offers angular resolution of 37 pixels per degree – more than Meta's current market-leading Quest VR headsets and enough to deliver crisp text and rich imagery.

The Meta VR Glasses can be used to play games or watch entertainment from the Meta Quest platform, including movies recorded in or converted to 3D. There are also new immersive formats that Meta is pioneering, like "immersive sports" streamed in ultra-high definition from the edge of the playing field at live events.

Users navigate the operating system using their eyes, voice and natural hand gestures like swiping and pinching, without having to use controllers – in some cases even to play entire games.

Meta also envisions the VR Glasses being used for work. Using full-colour passthrough – the view of the world in front of the glasses that's captured through its outward-facing cameras – wearers can turn any table surface into a keyboard and touchpad and surround themselves with multiple virtual screens from their Mac or PC.

The VR Glasses will deliver up to three hours of continuous media playback from the battery on the puck. Meta expects to put the device on sale in spring 2027.

Unlike the rest of Meta's eyewear offering, the VR glasses are not intended to be worn all the time or to be used primarily for AI assistance, although the company's new Muse AI will be built-in.

The use of Meta's AI glasses out on the street has earned them the nickname of "pervert glasses", due to various documented incidents of men using the barely visible camera to covertly film women.

Surveillance concerns were also amplified after a Swedish news investigation revealed that videos captured by wearers' cameras – including highly sensitive ones where they were nude or having sex – were being streamed to subcontractors in Kenya.

Read:

"Big Tech is using design philosophy as a smokescreen"

The pushback against these aspects of the technology may be a driver behind Meta's other key new product launch at Connect, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses.

Developed with long-term partners EssilorLuxottica, these glasses lack the controversial camera of other Meta models, as well as the small screen of the Meta Ray-Ban Displays, launched this time last year.

Their functionality is more limited, letting users listen to audio through small open‑ear directional speakers built into the frame and interact by voice with Meta's AI assistant.

The slimmer feature set has allowed Meta to introduce new slimmer styles like the partially wire-frame Ray-Ban Clubmaster. The glasses' 12-hour battery life and 43-gram weight also mean they can more easily be worn all day.

In addition to the new products, Meta revealed the Gen 3 version of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses, with three new frame silhouettes, and several new versions of the cheaper Meta Glasses, launched just three months ago, including one with pop star Lisa, whose influence is partly responsible for the Labubu craze.

The keynote presentation also detailed the expanding capabilities of its Muse "personal AI agent", which was first revealed two weeks ago and which the company will be adding to all of its glasses. At the end, there was a quick sneak peek at a new Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm gadget.

Meta has established itself as the dominant player in the small but growing market for AI glasses, accounting for 94 per cent of display-less AI glasses shipped in the first half of 2026, according to tracking by Counterpoint Research.

By the end of the year, it will have more than 100 different styles available in its Ray-Ban, Oakley and own-brand collections.

item.content:encoded:
As a wealthy nation, Norway has a responsibility to tackle climate change by developing a nature-first approach to designing buildings, Oslo Architecture Triennale director Line Ramstad tells Dezeen in this interview.

At this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale, built environment professionals and the general public gathered at Oslo's Sofienberg Church to discover architects' visions for prioritising nature through materials, design and planning.

Ramstad believes this discussion is long overdue.

"For a long time, we have needed to put nature first, but we are coming to a point where we can no longer close our eyes to it because otherwise there will be no future," she told Dezeen. "We need to take into consideration our position in the building industry and our ability to see solutions."

"Our green way of doing things is not really green"

Ramstad, a landscape architect from Norway, argued that the construction industry's current sustainability goals aren't doing enough to reduce carbon emissions and that a more circular, holistic approach to design is essential.

"We have started to talk about climate in our projects and our businesses, but we have tried to solve it within the system that created them, and more of the same doesn't solve anything," she said.

"Our green way of doing things is not really green. We lack the holistic thinking around this."

Norway in particular needs to confront its contribution to global warming, said Ramstad. She hopes that this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale will draw greater attention to the work required to mitigate the effects of climate change.

"Norway is a wonderful place to live – it's a rich country, but there's not that much willingness to change because things are going okay," said Ramstad.

"Having the triennale here is important for Norway to discuss internally what can be done – how can we shift our linear society to a circular one? Are there examples? Yes. Do we act within the system in a way that creates change? No."

"It's an important topic everywhere, but it's especially important here because we don't feel the consequences [of climate change] as directly as other places in the world," she continued. "It's time Norway realises that we also need to change."

Read:

Five stand-out projects at the Oslo Architecture Triennale

One project presented at the triennale exhibition that tackles Oslo's natural and built landscapes is General Plan 2.0 by Sigrid Legernes Teigen and Greta Gleisner Birkeland. It criticises years of building over historic waterways, which has contributed to increased flooding, and proposes a city plan that grows alongside the water.

"It's impressive what Sigrid and Greta have done," said Ramstad. "When rivers and wetlands become something we can build on, that's crazy."

"That's not putting nature first, and nature's natural forces will work against us, so what if we work with nature and plan our cities accordingly?"

Ramstad credits her fierce advocacy for designing with, not against, nature to her upbringing on a farm and her grandmother, who was a feminist and environmentalist.

In 2009, Ramstad founded non-profit architecture group Gyaw Gyaw and spent 15 years living on the Myanmar-Thailand border constructing buildings with local communities. It was here that her understanding of the effects of altering natural landscapes for construction crystallised.

"The results of our actions are so clear there," said Ramstad. "We built with local colleagues who have this closeness to what they're doing that we have lost a little here."

"Moving back to Norway was challenging after years of living in my jungle bubble."

"I have always had a sustainable approach, but coming back and meeting the reality in Norway, I was a little bit like, oh my God, we've gone far away in just 15 years," she continued. "We removed ourselves a lot from what my grandparents used to do."

"This triennale has made me more hopeful"

Although Ramstad's ambition of a nature-first future in the built environment sounds like a utopian dream, the work collected in the triennale has left her optimistic that this could one day be a more commonplace reality.

But, she acknowledged that systemic change in the industry is needed for architects' ecological proposals to become built projects.

"Working with this exhibition and this triennale has made me more hopeful than I was before because there is a great movement into thinking more holistically and circularly," said Ramstad.

"Architects are very concerned about [putting nature first], but when the system around an architect is not, it requires a lot for that office to implement a change by themselves."

"I hope that conversations here can inspire people to at least try, to get someone on board, see good examples and think, 'They did it there, so we can do it here'. We will make it, step by step."

item.content:encoded:
The latest edition of Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade, features pieces ranging from a pedestal constructed out of leftover shipping industry steel to a pagoda-like sculpture made from wooden trays.

This year's edition of the annual exhibition, which launched in 2008 to showcase Danish design, is currently taking place in the historic Charlottenborg Palace in central Copenhagen.

Here, curators Christian Hammer Juhl and Jade Chan of Christian + Jade have displayed works by ten Denmark-based designers in a fresco-covered room with a bare wooden floor that makes the pieces resemble artworks themselves.

While there are no specific parameters for which designers take part in The Mindcraft Project, the curators said that this year, it was quickly apparent that their picks all had something in common.

"We wanted to include designers at different stages of the career from different parts of Denmark, but also international designers who have been a part of shaping the Danish design scene," Chan told Dezeen.

"As our list grew, a very obvious red thread started to appear – there is a strong commitment to a special material or technique."

While Danish design is very well-known globally, the curators hope that The Mindcraft Project can help spotlight its less commercial side and give more of a focus on craft.

"We've always admired the platform and seen it as very important in Danish design culture because it gives a stage to more experimental and less commercially driven works," Juhl added.

"It gives a platform to people who are diving into craft and sort of lies in-between the craft and the design."

All the Mindcraft Project designers this year have a strong focus on their chosen material, with some choosing to show existing pieces and others creating entirely new work for this year's edition.

Among the latter were fashion designer Freya Dalsjø, whose Basket and Match Seat were painstakingly constructed from thin strands of leather, woven together to create a sculptural yet functional basket and seat or pillow.

"I was really honoured that they asked me; it's first and foremost an interior-focused exhibition, so it's super nice to be a part of it," Dalsjø told Dezeen.

"[Christian and Jade's] idea to ask me for these pieces was really good because the material worked – you can really see it in this context, in something other than fashion."

Designer Sigurd Nils Schelde also created new work for the exhibition, designing three pewter lamps that draw on architectural lighting.

"These works focus on different observations of architectural lighting from unfinished buildings; I was interested in how you see the light within a building," Schelde told Dezeen.

"It's like you're looking into the belly of the beast, and I was trying to adopt that into a more industrial language."

Schelde and Dalsjø's pieces are among some of this year's contributions that have a more polished, designed finish that clearly shows the work that went into refining the material, while other designers chose instead to highlight the raw materials.

Among them was Hans Severin Jacobsen, whose Untitled sculpture was made from oak and quartzite that the designer sourced from a gravel pit next to his studio in Jutland.

Jacobsen placed a rough-hewn 90-kilogram stone from the pit on a sleek oak base, cutting and squaring the sides of the stone to give it its final shape.

"I usually work with found stones where I leave some or all of the stone untouched, but with this piece I've worked to impose geometry on this natural stone," he told Dezeen. "So this is man-made geometry."

This focus on materiality was also evident in designer Daito Takefusa's piece Fragmented Signs (Double Touch B), which at first glance also appeared to be made from stone.

But the sculpture was made from ceramic, which Takefusa shaped with a rock to create its surface pattern before experimenting with different glazes, multiple layers of clay and oxides, to create an unusual, rough texture.

Read:

RCA design students exercise restraint in One Tool One Stool exhibition

"What's interesting for me is the process of firing and coming up with the final product – it resembles archaeology," he told Dezeen.

"I cover [the clay] with a material that doesn't melt, and after the firing, I brush it off," Takefusa continued. "It's akin to archaeological research; I never know what it's going to look like after the firing."

The products in The Mindraft Project exhibition flank a central piece by FOS, a room divider made from cast bronze with an organic design pattern made using hand tools.

In contrast, designer Anton Hendrik Denys' console and pedestal were made from readymade, leftover stainless steel from the furniture and shipping industry, which he combined using his knowledge of creating custom-made pieces for art galleries.

"The small chunky piece [in the pedestal] was for a bar stool for a super yacht, where they just needed a very thin piece of chunky stainless steel, and these pieces were disregarded afterwards," he told Dezeen.

"I asked what they had left and how we could put that together, and then the shape and the thickness of the material defined the end result. I haven't changed the shape of the leftover pieces; I only put them together."

Another notable piece was made by Lene Bødker, whose The Well design took months to make.

Using glass that she melts in a kiln before shaping it through a lost wax casting process, Bødker came up with an end design that was inspired by the wells of Rome as well as the healing powers of nature.

"This specific work is called The Well," Bødker told Dezeen. "It has no bottom; you can imagine it goes deep, deep down into the ground, and you can pull up this magical, healing holy water."

Near Bødker's piece is another design with a focus on water, designer Thomas Woltmann's ceramic-clad water fountain Helligkilden that features beautifully glossy tiles dyed with natural ochres.

As well as metal, stone, glass and leather, The Mindcraft Project also presented works in wood, including designer Anna Søgaard's functional products made from elm.

Her Curved Work, a set of trays and boxes, was made using a table saw to create a curved profile and then stacked to showcase their geometric shapes.

The boxes ended up resembling a pagoda, with the pattern of the grain showcasing Søgaard's attention to detail.

"I like boxes, storage that can contain things, but for me, it's about the sculptural way of working – I actually don't work with what you're putting inside, just the form of the box," she explained.

"It nearly looks like architecture, but this pagoda is actually just a single box and you can continue stacking it."

The final designer of this year's project, Nicholas Shurey, also worked with wood for his joyful Trio of Stools, Ziggy Pattern.

Partly inspired by designer Kansai Yamamoto's jumpsuit made for David Bowie, these sculptural seats bridge the gap between the sculptural and the functional, craft and design, neatly encompassing the theme of this year's exhibition.

Other recent design shows with a focus on materials include Hanging Baskets and One Tool One Stool at London Design Festival.

The photography is by Benjamin Lund.

The Mindcraft Project 2026 takes place at Charlottenborg Palace, Nyhavn 1, 1051 København K from 23 to 27 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

item.content:encoded:
On the heels of London Design Festival, we have rounded up a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste.

London Design Festival (LDF) concluded on Sunday, after a week of product launches, exhibitions and installations that showed the best of the capital's design scene.

Throughout the event, a trend that stood out was the presence of designers using materials leftover from manufacturing, whether as an attempt to slash costs, preserve resources or simply experiment visually.

Here are seven examples of the technique spotted during London's main design week:

Dagwood Bench by Lewis Duckworth

Lewis Duckworth is one of London's many emerging talents. As the co-founder of guerrilla collective Design Everything, he is always looking for ways to create furniture with the inevitable limitations that come with being a young, independent designer.

Dagwood Bench is one such project, made from timber end pieces leftover from furniture production, which are often too narrow or short to be reused and would normally go to waste.

Duckworth created the bench from a single laminated plank, sandwiched between two timber faces. The designer explained that offcuts were arranged within these pieces of wood to create a form that "appears visually thick while remaining lightweight and structurally capable".

"This project explores ways to re-evaluate these 'un-usable' elements by incorporating them into a larger, cohesive material system," he said. "Given that they started as an industrial byproduct, it felt most appropriate to reprocess them in a standardised format".

Duckworth's Dagwood Bench is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 Wood Award. A selection of these designs was on display at the Material Matters exhibition during LDF.

Second Song by Spared

Second Song is a selection of bird-shaped collectible objects by Brighton-based design studio Spared.

The studio is known for transforming waste generated by its varied clients into furniture and products, such as tables made from old coffee grounds developed for the Corner cafe at London's Tate Modern museum.

Cast using a selection of bio-based binders, the collectible birds were made of offcuts ranging from shell and stone to workshop sawdust and thin scrapings from the surfaces of plastic chopping boards used in industrial kitchens.

Second Song was another project presented at Material Matters.

Tissue box by Tom Golland

This statement tissue box was part of Out of Worky, an exhibition of bespoke pieces made using scrap materials that the participants had collected over years of taking on myriad jobs as emerging designers.

Tom Golland combined offcuts of walnut and white oak to form the unusually tall tissue dispenser, which is held together with two zinc-plated steel bolts.

The show was presented by The Worky, a collective founded by Marley Wellings, Jake Robertson, Kieran Slater and Milo Tonry-Brown.

Chair by Oscar Warman

Dubbed "everything I could find in my shed", this timber chair by emerging designer Oscar Warman is a Frankenstein-like hodgepodge of old pieces of furniture that were partially damaged.

The chair features a duo of rotten and frayed front legs, which had to be cut and altered.

This meant that Warman needed to source a strong piece of timber for the back legs, which he found in the form of part of a shelf that he "cannibalised" by taking it off the wall and using it alongside its brackets.

"By designing in this way I spent time mocking up and offering each part to one another to try and resemble a chair shape," said Warman.

"I like how few processes were used in the making of this piece and the time was spent problem solving how to make them function as a chair."

The chair is still on display as part of Design Everything's With Limitations show at Aram Gallery, which runs until 10 October.

Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester

Fused is one of a handful of lamps made by emerging designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester, who, quite literally, fused together different material offcuts from their respective practices to create lighting.

After Lester came across Grays's decorative glass experiments on Instagram, the designers combined the glass offcuts with scrap metal and electrical back boxes found in Lester's workshop. LED strips were pulled from old lamps to illuminate the pieces.

Also displayed at Aram Gallery, the rectilinear sconce lights are not the only pieces the duo made from offcuts that were on show during LDF. The pair also presented a chunky desk lamp as part of the Kiln Shift exhibition by Clink Street Ceramics.

Graywacke OffCut Chair by Carsten in der Elst

Based in Cologne, designer Carsten in der Elst has spent the last six years utilising "the full potential of industrial by-product material" when crafting pieces of furniture.

Central to In der Elst's portfolio is his Graywacke Offcut series – monolithic tables and chairs made from rough-hewn lumps of stone salvaged from a quarry in Lindlar, western Germany.

One of these ancient-looking chairs was presented as part of the Progressive Permanence exhibition by Max Radford Gallery at the Christopher Farr showroom in Shoreditch.

Coat rack by Duy Huynh

Emerging designer Duy Huynh is another exhibitor showing as part of With Limitations, who is presenting a timber coat rack made from offcuts salvaged from a stand he crafted to show work at his recent degree show.

The size of each piece of wood, reassembled by the designer, was determined by where the previous joints had been cut to create the stand.

"This piece is a bit smaller than a conventional coat rack, but I wanted to keep that acknowledgement of where it came from to show the idea that if we treat our materials right, they can serve us for a long time," said Huynh.

London Design Festival 2026 took place at various locations around the city from 12 to 20 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.
